title: Google Builds A New Gemini Model Team As AI Investments Accelerate
gist: Jeff Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, Quoc Le and Oriol Vinyals are leaving Google for AI-for-science startup Discovery Loop while Demis Hassabis takes the chief scientist role and Koray Kavukcuoglu takes over Gemini, which Morgan reads as Google forcibly rebuilding a Gemini team it is unhappy with after Gemini 3.5 Pro slipped from its June ship date. Simultaneously Google is raising 2026 capex guidance to $195-205 billion, reportedly floating a $25 billion bond, and posting a Google Cloud inflection: Q2 revenue up 81.8 percent to $24.77 billion at a record 35.6 percent operating margin against a $514 billion backlog.

insights.claim: Jeff Dean is leaving Google after 27 years to head Discovery Loop, an AI startup automating scientific research workflows, and is taking three senior AI researchers with him: Sanjay Ghemawat, Quoc Le and Oriol Vinyals.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The simultaneous departure of Google's most senior systems and deep-learning architects is a talent-concentration risk for Gemini and a signal to watch Discovery Loop as a new AI-for-science entrant.
insights.locator: Significantly, Jeff Dean, who was employee

insights.claim: Google is taking an investment stake in Discovery Loop, the startup its departing AI leadership is founding, rather than treating the exit as a clean break.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Equity in the spinout keeps Google optionality on AI-for-science without funding it on-balance-sheet, and follows the pattern of hyperscalers booking startup stakes as investments.
insights.locator: Google is making an investment in Discovery Loop

insights.claim: The friendly framing of the Google AI executive departures is cover: the company is constructing a new Gemini team because it is dissatisfied with the output of the existing one.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Reads the reshuffle as a performance-driven purge rather than voluntary attrition, implying Gemini's roadmap slippage is being addressed at the org level and could take quarters to fix.
insights.quote: clearly Google is building a new Gemini team because it is not happy with what it is getting out of the current team
insights.locator: Google is making an investment in Discovery Loop

insights.claim: Google's flagship Gemini 3.5 Pro was announced in May and expected to ship in June but remains unavailable with no delivery date given.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A concrete, dateable frontier-model slip at Google is the cleanest evidence available that its model roadmap is behind, and a checkpoint for anyone tracking Gemini-versus-Claude/GPT share.
insights.locator: Moreover, Google's top-end Gemini model is falling behind

insights.claim: Google's top-end Gemini model is falling behind Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's GPT despite Google having invented the transformer architecture that underpins all generative AI models.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Architectural invention has not translated into frontier leadership, undercutting the assumption that incumbency in research guarantees model-quality moats.
insights.locator: Moreover, Google's top-end Gemini model is falling behind

insights.claim: The push toward AGI has itself become a source of model release delays across AI builders, because models misbehave or exhibit emergent behaviors that are hard to guardrail.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Frames frontier-model launch slippage as a structural feature of the AGI race, not a company-specific failure — expect schedule risk to persist at OpenAI and Anthropic too.
insights.quote: the push towards AGI has caused delays in models being released because the models do not behave appropriately, or have bad emergent behaviors that are difficult to guardrail
insights.locator: Despite the enormous progress that has been made

insights.claim: A plausible motive for Google's senior AI researchers leaving is a desire to work on something not at hyperscale and unambiguously beneficial, since accelerating scientific discovery is more benign than building AGI that will replace far more people than it augments.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Mission-driven attrition is a recurring retention risk for labs pursuing AGI, and points to AI-for-science as the destination category absorbing that talent.
insights.locator: But, it is also possible that in addition to this

insights.claim: Demis Hassabis is moving up to chairman of DeepMind and taking the Google chief scientist job from Jeff Dean, while Koray Kavukcuoglu, DeepMind's former CTO, becomes Google's chief AI architect in charge of the Gemini models.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Names the specific people now accountable for Gemini's trajectory — the decision chain to watch for any recovery in Google's model competitiveness.
insights.locator: Now, Demis Hassabis, who was one of the co-founders

insights.claim: Replacing a longtime hardware and software infrastructure leader with one of the world's top AI research minds as Google's chief scientist marks a deliberate shift in the company's center of gravity from systems engineering to AI research.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Suggests future Google differentiation is being bet on model research rather than infrastructure advantage, even as TPU and datacenter spend hits records.
insights.quote: It is important to note that the longtime hardware and software infrastructure guy (Dean) is being replaced by one of top AI minds in the world (Hassabis).
insights.locator: It is important to note that the longtime hardware

insights.claim: Google's decades-long maintenance of two parallel AI research organizations, DeepMind and Google Brain, has produced fiefdoms and infighting rather than useful competition, and the reshuffle effectively ends it with DeepMind on top.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Org consolidation should shorten research-to-production cycles at Google; watch whether Gemini release cadence improves as the duplicate structure collapses.
insights.quote: From where I sit, it looks like DeepMind won and Google Brain left the building.
insights.locator: Here's the thing. DeepMind has been kept distinct

insights.claim: In the AGI race the binding constraint is getting research into production as fast as possible, which argues for a single consolidated AI group rather than competing internal teams.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for judging any AI lab's org chart: duplicated research units are a productivity tax when time-to-production is what wins.
insights.quote: Google needs to have one AI group and get focused.
insights.locator: GenAI and the race towards AGI means putting research

insights.claim: Amin Vahdat, chief technologist for AI infrastructure and architect of many of Google's networking innovations, remains firmly in charge of Google infrastructure as a senior vice president through the AI leadership shakeup.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Infrastructure continuity means the TPU and networking roadmap is insulated from the model-team turmoil — capex execution risk is lower than headline exec churn implies.
insights.locator: Amin Vahdat, who is chief technologist for AI infrastructure

insights.claim: Google raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance from $180-190 billion to $195-205 billion, with CFO Anat Ashkenazi attributing the increase mostly to pulling planned capacity forward into 2026 rather than to infrastructure price increases.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Pull-forward rather than inflation means real incremental unit demand for servers, networking and datacenters in 2026 — bullish for the supply chain, and it borrows from 2027 volumes.
insights.locator: In its financial report from last week

insights.claim: Google is reportedly seeking a $25 billion bond offering to fund its AI infrastructure investments rather than draining its cash pile.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Even the most cash-rich hyperscaler is now terming out AI capex in the debt market — watch hyperscaler issuance as a supply factor in corporate credit.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the AI buildout continues

insights.claim: Google spent $44.92 billion on capital expenses in the second quarter, all of it for Google Cloud, split roughly 60 percent on servers ($26.95 billion) and 40 percent on datacenters and networking ($17.97 billion) — almost precisely 2X the year-ago level in both buckets.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The stable 60/40 server-versus-facility split doubling year on year gives a clean sizing ratio for allocating hyperscaler capex between compute vendors and datacenter/network suppliers.
insights.locator: In the quarter, Google spent $44.92 billion

insights.claim: Google's capex level is driven entirely by a Google Cloud backlog that stood at $514 billion at the end of the second quarter, up 4.75X year on year and 11.3 percent sequentially.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Backlog is the leading indicator for Google capex — a stall in sequential backlog growth would be the first warning that the buildout decelerates.
insights.quote: That capex level is driven entirely by the Google Cloud backlog, which was at $514 billion as the second quarter came to a close
insights.locator: That capex level is driven entirely by the Google Cloud backlog

insights.claim: Google internally treats the network as part of the datacenter enclosure rather than part of the server racks, reflecting a decades-old view that a datacenter is itself just one big server.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Explains why Google's disclosed capex splits put networking with facilities, which matters when comparing its spending mix to other hyperscalers' reporting conventions.
insights.quote: A datacenter is just a big server to Google, and has been for decades.
insights.locator: It is funny how the network is part of the datacenter enclosure

insights.claim: Google Cloud second-quarter revenue rose 81.8 percent year on year to $24.77 billion and grew 23.7 percent sequentially from Q1 2026.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Sequential growth near 24 percent implies the AI demand curve is still steepening rather than plateauing — a live read on cloud AI consumption.
insights.locator: In the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue was up 81.8 percent

insights.claim: Google Cloud operating income rose 3.1X to $8.81 billion, a record 35.6 percent operating margin, turning a unit that dragged on Google's profits for years into a support for them.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: AI cloud workloads are proving highly margin-accretive at scale, contradicting the view that AI serving is structurally low-margin.
insights.locator: Operating income for the cloud group rose by a factor of 3.1X

insights.claim: Google Cloud reached 20.7 percent of Google's overall revenue and 21.6 percent of its operating income in the second quarter, both new highs.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Cloud now contributes a larger share of profit than of revenue for the first time, shifting the valuation mix of Alphabet away from pure search advertising.
insights.locator: By the way, Google Cloud represented 20.7 percent

insights.claim: The profitability of Google's non-cloud businesses is what funds the cloud and AI buildout, providing both the cash and the borrowing capacity that keeps the company from burning down its cash hoard.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Any deterioration in search or ads profitability transmits directly into AI capex capacity — the two are not independent lines to model.
insights.locator: The health of the overall Google businesses matters

insights.claim: Alphabet's second-quarter revenues rose 24.2 percent to $119.8 billion and operating income rose 30.4 percent to $40.77 billion.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Operating income growing faster than revenue at a $120 billion quarterly base shows the AI spending surge has not yet compressed core operating leverage.
insights.locator: Overall, Google's revenues

insights.claim: Google's reported net income was up nearly 4X to $112.11 billion, but roughly $77.1 billion of that came from mark-to-market gains on investments, leaving underlying net income on the order of $35 billion.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Headline EPS at Google is now dominated by non-operating marks — model the ~$35 billion underlying figure, and expect the same distortion to reverse if private AI and space valuations fall.
insights.locator: The underlying net income for all of Google

insights.claim: Across big cloud builders and IT suppliers that invested in AI model builders, net income is increasingly composed of paper gains, making it hard to reckon how the underlying business actually performed.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A cross-sector screening rule: strip investment marks out of hyperscaler and IT-supplier net income before comparing earnings growth or valuation multiples.
insights.quote: net income is starting to become largely paper gains, which makes it had to reckon how the underlying company really did
insights.locator: With the big cloud builders and IT suppliers

insights.claim: The bulk of Google's investment gains came from a $94 billion holding in SpaceX, with additional contribution from its stake in Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Alphabet's earnings now carry direct beta to SpaceX and Anthropic valuations, an under-appreciated correlation for anyone hedging Alphabet exposure.
insights.locator: A lot of this funny money came from a $94 billion holding

insights.claim: SpaceX went public last month and its stock initially rose because Google was renting capacity on the SpaceX Colossus supercomputer for $920 million a month.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: An $11 billion annualized compute rental from Google to SpaceX creates a circular revenue-and-stake loop that flatters both the holding's mark and SpaceX's revenue line.

themes.theme: Pichai's Framing Of The AGI Push

insights.claim: Sundar Pichai justified the AI executive reorganization by calling for acceleration and frontier focus, framing the moment as uniquely important for shaping the future of AGI and science.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The CEO's own language ties the reorg to urgency rather than routine succession, corroborating the read that Google believes it is behind.
insights.quote: We have to accelerate all this work and stay focused on the AI frontier,
insights.locator: Google chief executive officer Sundar Pichai explained in a blog post

insights.claim: Pichai says Hassabis has described Google as standing in the foothills of the singularity and had been spending much of his time engaging externally, prompting a role change that lets him focus fully on shaping AGI.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Signals Google intends Hassabis as both its AGI strategist and external face, concentrating narrative control over Google's AI story in one person.
